items.title: Agent Error Dataset: Scaling 50,000 Error--Diagnosis Pairs for Failure Analysis and Error-Aware Post-Training
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Agent Error Dataset (AED), a large collection of 50,000 error-diagnosis pairs for text-based LLM agents. The core method involves a five-stage pipeline (AET) to automatically identify agent failures, diagnose their causes, and propose corrections using existing execution traces. The main contribution is providing a scalable resource for analyzing agent failures and developing error-aware post-training techniques, enabling agents to learn from their mistakes without re-running entire rollouts.

items.title: PhantomEnvironments: Training LLM Agents in Fictional Worlds
items.abstract: This paper introduces PhantomEnvironments, a novel method for training LLM agents using purely rule-based, fictional environments. This approach bypasses the need for costly human data or LLM-generated environments prone to hallucinations. The core contribution is demonstrating that agents trained in these synthetic worlds can effectively transfer their multi-hop search capabilities to real-world tasks, even outperforming agents trained on real data.
items.figure_caption: LLM agents trained with RL in PhantomEnvironments transfer to real-world search.

items.title: PivotOPD: Learning to Recover from Pivotal Mistakes in Multi-Turn Agents
items.abstract: PivotOPD addresses the compounding errors in multi-turn language agents by identifying and correcting "pivotal mistakes" – actions that significantly derail task progress. The core method involves an on-policy distillation framework that trains agents to both avoid these critical errors and recover from the states they induce. This approach aims to improve task success by focusing on early intervention and guided recovery after crucial missteps.

items.title: Debias It Yourself: Teaching LLMs Cognitive Bias Mitigation Interventions
items.abstract: This paper introduces "Debias It Yourself" (DIY), a framework that translates human cognitive bias mitigation techniques into methods for large language models. The core method involves applying these interventions through in-context examples, instruction tuning, or guided self-revision. The key contribution is demonstrating that these cognitively grounded approaches significantly reduce bias in LLMs while maintaining high reasoning accuracy, even on novel bias types.
items.figure_caption: Example of a cognitive bias-reduction intervention using counter-stereotypical imaging.

items.title: JuryFlow: Disagreement-Guided Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Evaluation
items.abstract: JuryFlow addresses the unreliability of LLM judges by treating inter-judge disagreement as a valuable signal. Its core method decomposes responses into atomic claims, uses heterogeneous judges to provide per-claim verdicts, and builds a disagreement graph. The framework's contribution is a human-in-the-loop system that guides minimal human interventions to resolve specific disagreements, improving evaluation accuracy.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. Conceptual overview of JuryFlow. Multiple LLM Agents extract Claims from a candidate response and produce per-claim verdicts, forming a Disagreement Graph that surfaces conflicts. A Human selects the most critical disagreement point—the only human intervention (made automatically by entropy ranking in our experiments). The system then performs Propagated Re-Evaluation across related claims and historical cases, and abstracts the correction into a Rubric Update that all agents inherit, closing the loop. A conceptual illustration showing the JuryFlow pipeline from left to right. Three AI robot icons (labeled Agents) each produce a document icon (labeled Claim). Arrows flow from agents and claims into a central disagreement graph, a dense network of interconnected nodes with some edges highlighted in amber to indicate conflict. A human selects the highest-entropy focal node (automated in our experiments). Dashed arrows lead rightward to a second, lighter graph representing Propagated Re-Evaluation, and finally to a checklist document icon labeled Rubric Update.

items.title: Persistent Context Graphs for Efficient Memory Compaction in LLM Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces ReCAP, a novel method for efficient memory compaction in LLM agents. ReCAP constructs a persistent context graph storing attention-derived importance scores and message dependencies. This allows agents to quickly identify and retrieve relevant past interactions for new requests without re-encoding expired KV caches, significantly reducing computational costs and improving long-horizon task performance.
items.figure_caption: ReCAP preserves attention-derived importance and dependency links in a persistent context graph. For each new request, it combines stored importance with the request’s relevance cues to select historical blocks and their supporting context, retaining protected contexts.

items.title: Cogentic: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Automated Proof Discovery
items.abstract: Cogentic is a multi-agent system designed for automated proof discovery on complex, open research problems. Its core method involves an iterative prove-verify loop where an orchestrator manages multiple independent "provers" exploring different mathematical directions. These proofs are then rigorously verified by specialized components, and confirmed intermediate results are stored to build upon in subsequent rounds, enabling the system to tackle challenging math and theoretical computer science problems.

items.title: ComputerSD: Online Self-Distillation from Real-Time Feedback for Computer-Use Agents
items.abstract: ComputerSD addresses the challenge of sparse rewards in training computer-use agents by introducing online self-distillation. It leverages real-time feedback from GUI transitions to generate privileged guidance and a step-level value score. This dual approach allows for token-level learning from the guidance while regulating the learning
items.figure_caption: Motivation and preliminaries. (a) Comparison of GRPO, OPSD and ComputerSD. During online training, we measure (b) suppressed ratio (the ratio of tokens at correct steps whose log-probability is lowered) under fixed guidance and real-time feedback and (c) conflict ratio (the ratio of tokens whose shift contradicts the step-level judgment) in correct and incorrect steps.

items.title: cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces `cua-speedrun`, a standardized benchmarking framework for evaluating the speed and efficiency of computer-use agents (CUAs). It addresses the reproducibility crisis in CUA benchmarks by providing a uniform virtual machine setup and execution pipeline. `cua-speedrun`'s core contribution is enabling reliable speed comparisons of CUAs, crucial for their wider adoption.

items.title: EviRover: Reinforcing Agentic Perception Beyond a Glance
items.abstract: This paper introduces EviRover, a novel agentic perception system that overcomes the limitations of single-glance visual analysis. Its core method involves training an agent to interactively gather more information beyond an initial observation, addressing "perception under insufficient evidence." The key contribution is the creation of new datasets and the EviRover agent itself, designed to learn this interactive perception process.
items.figure_caption: Representative examples from our training data and the EviLens benchmark.

items.title: Learning from Research: Toward Lifelong Agent Harness Evolution
items.abstract: This paper introduces ScholarEvolve, a framework for continually improving language agents by evolving their "harness" (tool use, memory, execution logic) without retraining the core language model. Its core method involves using topic modeling on research literature to identify and implement novel improvement strategies for different harness modules, enabling proactive and exploratory adaptation. The main contribution is a system that leverages external research knowledge to guide harness evolution, overcoming limitations of purely reactive, feedback-driven methods.
items.figure_caption: Overview of ScholarEvolve . Left: workflow focused exploration. Middle: research guided module mutation, recombination, and lifelong evolution. Right: Qwen3.5-27B task (TGC) and scenario (SGC) goal completion on AppWorld Challenge.

items.title: What Can Component-Replacement Evidence Establish? A Critical Scoping Review of Local Decisions in LLM Agents
items.abstract: This paper critically reviews how component replacement evidence is used to evaluate LLM agents. It finds that while many studies report local decision metrics and task outcomes, few establish a clear causal link between the two due to insufficient matched comparisons. The core contribution is highlighting the need for better experimental design to accurately assess the impact of local decision quality on overall task performance.

items.title: Who Verifies the Graph? Misspecification Attacks on Causal Action Verification for Language Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces "misspecification attacks" that exploit vulnerabilities in causal action verifiers used by language agents. By subtly corrupting the underlying causal graph, these attacks can trick verifiers into approving harmful actions, even though the verifier issues a seemingly valid certificate. The authors propose an attestation step to detect such attacks by cross-referencing certified executions with randomized samples.

items.title: OpenTSLM TeeMoE: A Unified Time-Series Language Model for Forecasting, Contextual Prediction, and Reasoning
items.abstract: OpenTSLM TeeMoE is a unified time-series language model that addresses the fragmentation of current models by integrating forecasting, contextual prediction, and temporal reasoning. Its core method involves a mixture-of-experts architecture with three specialized, low-rank experts for aggregation, native forecasting, and temporal analysis, controlled by a learned weighting mechanism. The key contribution is enabling a single model to perform these diverse time-series tasks effectively, even synthesizing predictions from external numerical specialists.

items.title: EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: EvoDuet addresses LLM limitations in scientific discovery by co-evolving solutions and search queries. It uses a retrieval gate to dynamically decide when to search for new information or reuse existing documents based on knowledge gaps. This bilevel optimization significantly improves discovery gain for some LLMs by intelligently guiding web searches to yield more relevant documents for problem-solving.
items.figure_caption: Packing loops of multiple optimization scaffolds

items.abstract: This paper introduces Fenchel Tilt Flow Control (FTFC), a novel method for efficiently fine-tuning generative models to align with arbitrary utility functions. FTFC decouples utility optimization from model fitting by learning

SW 1 is distance to the independent numerical target (right, ground truth). FTFC converges faster to target according to the utility function. Comparison is made with FDC ( de2025flow ) and ITM ( potaptchik2025tilt ) . See Section 4.1 for details.

items.title: Game-Guided Skill Discovery through Self-Play for Playable Agent Control
items.abstract: This paper introduces Game-Guided Skill Discovery (GGSD), a framework that leverages self-play in games to learn human-playable motor skills. By training a hierarchical agent to compete against itself, GGSD discovers semantically distinct and interpretable skills that act as compact behavioral abstractions for agent control. The core contribution is enabling direct human control of agents using a small set of learned, playable skills, leading to emergent complex behaviors through skill transitions.
items.figure_caption: Different game rules guide agents toward different playable skills. Shown are gameplay snapshots of agents learned with GGSD.

items.title: Grounding Time-Series Foundation Models in Digital Twin Topology for Predictive Maintenance
items.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of applying time-series foundation models (TSFMs) to predictive maintenance within digital twins. The core method involves benchmarking existing TSFMs and proposing a novel topology-informed fusion approach. The main contribution is demonstrating that multivariate TSFMs perform better for remaining useful life prediction in digital twins and introducing a method to leverage digital twin topology for improved adaptation.
items.figure_caption: Digital twin framework for standardized development.

items.title: Inference Auctions
items.abstract: This paper proposes an "inference auction" to address compute capacity limitations for LLM APIs. The core method is an auction mechanism that allows users to bid for faster inference service, efficiently allocating priority without sacrificing latency. The key contribution is a system that enables economically efficient priority allocation, incentivizes truthful bidding through fast algorithms, and includes an autobidding agent to maximize user utility within budget constraints, ultimately increasing system welfare.

papers.figure_caption: Motivation and preliminaries. (a) Comparison of GRPO, OPSD and ComputerSD. During online training, we measure (b) suppressed ratio (the ratio of tokens at correct steps whose log-probability is lowered) under fixed guidance and real-time feedback and (c) conflict ratio (the ratio of tokens whose shift contradicts the step-level judgment) in correct and incorrect steps.

papers.title: cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces `cua-speedrun`, a standardized benchmarking framework for evaluating the speed and efficiency of computer-use agents (CUAs). It addresses the reproducibility crisis in CUA benchmarks by providing a uniform virtual machine setup and execution pipeline. `cua-speedrun`'s core contribution is enabling reliable speed comparisons of CUAs, crucial for their wider adoption.

papers.title: EviRover: Reinforcing Agentic Perception Beyond a Glance
papers.abstract: This paper introduces EviRover, a novel agentic perception system that overcomes the limitations of single-glance visual analysis. Its core method involves training an agent to interactively gather more information beyond an initial observation, addressing "perception under insufficient evidence." The key contribution is the creation of new datasets and the EviRover agent itself, designed to learn this interactive perception process.
papers.figure_caption: Representative examples from our training data and the EviLens benchmark.

papers.title: Learning from Research: Toward Lifelong Agent Harness Evolution
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ScholarEvolve, a framework for continually improving language agents by evolving their "harness" (tool use, memory, execution logic) without retraining the core language model. Its core method involves using topic modeling on research literature to identify and implement novel improvement strategies for different harness modules, enabling proactive and exploratory adaptation. The main contribution is a system that leverages external research knowledge to guide harness evolution, overcoming limitations of purely reactive, feedback-driven methods.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of ScholarEvolve . Left: workflow focused exploration. Middle: research guided module mutation, recombination, and lifelong evolution. Right: Qwen3.5-27B task (TGC) and scenario (SGC) goal completion on AppWorld Challenge.

papers.title: What Can Component-Replacement Evidence Establish? A Critical Scoping Review of Local Decisions in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: This paper critically reviews how component replacement evidence is used to evaluate LLM agents. It finds that while many studies report local decision metrics and task outcomes, few establish a clear causal link between the two due to insufficient matched comparisons. The core contribution is highlighting the need for better experimental design to accurately assess the impact of local decision quality on overall task performance.

papers.title: Who Verifies the Graph? Misspecification Attacks on Causal Action Verification for Language Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "misspecification attacks" that exploit vulnerabilities in causal action verifiers used by language agents. By subtly corrupting the underlying causal graph, these attacks can trick verifiers into approving harmful actions, even though the verifier issues a seemingly valid certificate. The authors propose an attestation step to detect such attacks by cross-referencing certified executions with randomized samples.

papers.title: OpenTSLM TeeMoE: A Unified Time-Series Language Model for Forecasting, Contextual Prediction, and Reasoning
papers.abstract: OpenTSLM TeeMoE is a unified time-series language model that addresses the fragmentation of current models by integrating forecasting, contextual prediction, and temporal reasoning. Its core method involves a mixture-of-experts architecture with three specialized, low-rank experts for aggregation, native forecasting, and temporal analysis, controlled by a learned weighting mechanism. The key contribution is enabling a single model to perform these diverse time-series tasks effectively, even synthesizing predictions from external numerical specialists.

papers.title: EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: EvoDuet addresses LLM limitations in scientific discovery by co-evolving solutions and search queries. It uses a retrieval gate to dynamically decide when to search for new information or reuse existing documents based on knowledge gaps. This bilevel optimization significantly improves discovery gain for some LLMs by intelligently guiding web searches to yield more relevant documents for problem-solving.

papers.title: Fenchel Tilting: Weighted Correction for Efficient Finetuning of Generative Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Fenchel Tilt Flow Control (FTFC), a novel method for efficiently fine-tuning generative models to align with arbitrary utility functions. FTFC decouples utility optimization from model fitting by learning
papers.figure_caption: Left-tail CVaR on two rings. Gold bands correspond to d ⁡ ( x ) ≤ 0.15 d(x)\( \leq \) 0.15 . L L counts number of sampling steps. SW 1 is distance to the independent numerical target (right, ground truth). FTFC converges faster to target according to the utility function. Comparison is made with FDC ( de2025flow ) and ITM ( potaptchik2025tilt ) . See Section 4.1 for details.

papers.title: Game-Guided Skill Discovery through Self-Play for Playable Agent Control
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Game-Guided Skill Discovery (GGSD), a framework that leverages self-play in games to learn human-playable motor skills. By training a hierarchical agent to compete against itself, GGSD discovers semantically distinct and interpretable skills that act as compact behavioral abstractions for agent control. The core contribution is enabling direct human control of agents using a small set of learned, playable skills, leading to emergent complex behaviors through skill transitions.
papers.figure_caption: Different game rules guide agents toward different playable skills. Shown are gameplay snapshots of agents learned with GGSD.

papers.title: Grounding Time-Series Foundation Models in Digital Twin Topology for Predictive Maintenance
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of applying time-series foundation models (TSFMs) to predictive maintenance within digital twins. The core method involves benchmarking existing TSFMs and proposing a novel topology-informed fusion approach. The main contribution is demonstrating that multivariate TSFMs perform better for remaining useful life prediction in digital twins and introducing a method to leverage digital twin topology for improved adaptation.
papers.figure_caption: Digital twin framework for standardized development.

papers.title: How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the necessity of complex "harnesses" for autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents. The core finding is that advanced, multi-agent orchestrators offer no significant advantage over a simple

papers.title: Inference Auctions
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an "inference auction" to address compute capacity limitations for LLM APIs. The core method is an auction mechanism that allows users to bid for faster inference service, efficiently allocating priority without sacrificing latency. The key contribution is a system that enables economically efficient priority allocation, incentivizes truthful bidding through fast algorithms, and includes an autobidding agent to maximize user utility within budget constraints, ultimately increasing system welfare.
